# Sulphuric acid (oil of vitriol) (`sulphuric_acid`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: needs distillation; helped by saltpetre_production, glassmaking
- Core idea: Green vitriol (iron sulphate, from weathered pyrites) first dried, then heated to red heat in a clay retort, gives off white fumes that condense to a heavy, oily, corrosive acid. The cheaper way: burn sulphur with about one eighth its weight of saltpetre over a little water inside a closed vessel, first a glass bell, from 1746 a lead-lined room (lead resists the acid), and boil the weak acid down in glass. It is the key to nitric and hydrochloric acid, soda, ether and fertiliser, so cheap sulphuric acid opens the whole of chemistry.
- Pitfalls:
  - Pouring water into the strong acid: it boils explosively and spits. Always add the acid slowly to the water.
  - The acid chars skin, cloth and wood at once; the fumes of burning sulphur damage the lungs.
  - Confusing the vitriols: green is iron, blue is copper, white is zinc.
  - Using iron or copper vessels for the dilute acid; they dissolve. Glass, stoneware and lead hold it.
- History: islamic: 8th–10th c. – vitriols and their distillates handled by Jabirian authors and al-Razi; that they isolated the acid is often claimed but disputed; india: c. 12th–16th c. – alchemical texts describe distilling vitriols and alum; isolation of the acid is uncertain; europe: c. 1300 – distillates of vitriol in pseudo-Geber and Vincent of Beauvais; 16th c. clear recipes (Cordus, Libavius); 1746 Roebuck's lead chamber; 1831 Phillips patents the contact process, industrial from the 1890s
- Read:
  - Vladimír Karpenko & John A. Norris, Vitriol in the History of Chemistry, Chemické listy 96 (2002)
  - Archibald Clow & Nan L. Clow, The Chemical Revolution (1952)
